 Why I trust our elections
 A Kenton County poll worker responds to the accusations and conjecture about our elections
 ,  
  and  
 Guest Author 
 November 8, 2026
 Share -->
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on BlueSky 
 Share on LinkedIn 
 Share on Reddit 
 Share via Email 
 For those who question every single aspect of how voters can vote and how those votes are counted in this county and in Kentucky, you have my sympathy.
 I am utterly amazed at how some people can endlessly obsess about a process that is as highly scrutinized and regulated as elections are in this state. Their incessant nattering for “proof” absent any supporting evidence that problems actually exist is exhausting.
 To the contrary, there is overwhelming proof that elections are fairly and equitably administered in Kenton County and across the state.
 Here’s one example: During last week’s three days of no-excuse early voting, over 17,000 voters from all over Kenton County cast their ballots using the wildly successful ballot-on-demand (BOD) system.
 Printing costs, undoubtedly, would have been astronomical if the county attempted to provide pre-printed ballots for every precinct at every voting center.
 Yet some people cling to the nonsensical position that paper ballots aren’t real paper ballots unless voters “bubble in” their selections with an ink pen. They seem to ignore the fact that pre-printed ballots are optically scanned just like the BOD paper ballots. And both types of paper ballots create a —you guessed it — traceable paper trail.
 Ballot-on-demand increases voter access, saves taxpayer money, and is more equitable for all voters regardless of where they live or work. Voters don’t have to play beat-the-clock to get across Kenton County to a specific precinct before the polls close.
 Last week, they could choose from any of five polling locations most convenient to them or less crowded. And on Nov. 3rd voters can use their assigned precinct or go to any of the county’s 32 polling sites. Why? Because Kenton County provides ballot-on-demand everywhere!
 The bottom line is that no one can cast a vote in any Kentucky county without using a paper ballot. End of story. 
 Other naysayers try and cast suspicion about basic, foundational technology that allows votes to be counted efficiently, effectively and securely … by machine. (News flash: Modern society ditched the abacus a long time ago.)
 No voting machine in the state is connected to the internet. None. Anywhere. Anytime.
 And, by the way, county election officials have the ability and can be required by law to cross-check machine tallies by physically counting the paper ballots to verify the results.
 Anyone in Kentucky who has taken the time to work as an election official knows what it’s like to take the training, understand the voting process, and be willing to meet the mostly-friendly public at the polls for up to 12 hours a day. We do it because we believe in our neighbors, our communities, and the right to vote.
 So election deniers, I offer you my thoughts and prayers because the dark, suspicious world in which you choose to live must be frightening.
 But you don’t need to take a leap of faith to have confidence in our election process. You can learn to trust again! Sign up to be an election official next season. Education is enlightening.
 --30-- 
 Written by Becky Jones, a poll worker in Kenton County.
